title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Monolith vs Microservices
summary: A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's logic, while microservices decompose that logic into many small, independently deployable services that communicate over a network — trading operational…
objectives: What is the core difference between a monolith and microservices, and why is "deployable unit" the right boundary?
When should you start with a monolith, and when does the decomposition become worth its cost?
Why is sharing a database across microservices considered an anti-pattern?
How do cross-service transactions work when each service owns its own database?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's logic, while microservices decompose that logic into many small, independently deployable services that communicate over a network — trading operational simplicity for deployment agility and team autonomy.

A monolithic application is the default architecture for any new system: all modules — UI rendering, business logic, data access, background jobs — live in one process, share one memory space, and ship as one artifact. This is not a defect; it is the correct starting point because it minimizes the cost of change. When three engineers are building an MVP, a monolith lets them refactor across module boundaries without coordinating deployments, share function calls instead of network hops, and debug the whole system in a single debugger. Amazon in 2001 was a monolith — the "obidos" codebase — and it worked until it didn't: by the time Bezos issued his famous "every team must expose its data through an API" mandate, the obidos codebase had grown so tangled that no single engineer understood it, every change risked breaking an unrelated feature, and deployments required coordinating across dozens of teams that all shared one release train. The monolith had become an organizational bottleneck, not a technical one.

Microservices invert this. Each business capability — billing, inventory, recommendations, search, playback — becomes its own service with its own codebase, its own database, its own deployment pipeline, and its own on-call rotation. Teams own services end-to-end and can ship multiple times per day without coordinating with anyone else. Netflix, after its 2008–2010 migration off a single Oracle database into hundreds of Cassandra-backed microservices, went from monthly deployments to thousands of deployments per day; Uber followed the same arc, growing from a monolithic "Rails monolith" called "API" into roughly 2,200 microservices by 2019. The benefit is Conway's Law made explicit: the architecture mirrors the org chart, and a team that owns a service can move at its own pace. The cost is a dramatic increase in operational complexity — distributed tracing, service discovery, circuit breakers, saga-based transactions, and partial-failure handling all become first-class engineering concerns.

The trade-off is sharp on three axes. **Deployment**: a monolith deploys as one artifact, so version skew is impossible but every deploy risks the whole system; microservices deploy independently, so partial rollouts are safe but version skew across services is constant and must be designed for (typically with backward-compatible API changes and consumer-driven contracts). **Performance**: in-process function calls take nanoseconds, while cross-service network calls take milliseconds, so a single user request that fans out to ten services adds 50–100ms of pure network overhead; this is why Netflix's edge API gateway aggressively caches and aggregates. **Failure mode**: a monolith fails as a unit, so the blast radius is all-or-nothing, but recovery is one rollback; microservices fail partially, so one service's outage must be isolated by circuit breakers and fallbacks, but recovery can be a single-service redeploy. The architect's rule, popularized by Martin Fowler's "monolith-first" essay, is to start with a monolith, decompose only when the org chart forces it (typically above ~50 engineers or when one team's deploy cadence is blocked by another), and to decompose along business-capability lines, not technical-layer lines (so "billing" is one service, not "data access layer").

The most common decomposition mistake is splitting too early or too finely. A team of 5 that splits its MVP into 12 microservices spends more time on operational plumbing than on features, and the latency of cross-service calls makes the product slower than the monolith it replaced. The second most common mistake is sharing a database across services — this creates hidden coupling where a schema change in one service breaks another, defeating the entire point of decomposition. The third is failing to invest in observability: a microservices system without distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray) is effectively undebuggable, because a single user request may touch 20 services and the failure could be in any of them. The architect's checklist before decomposing: do you have more than ~50 engineers? Do you have CI/CD per service? Do you have distributed tracing? Do you have an API gateway or service mesh? Do you have a story for cross-service transactions (saga or outbox)? If any answer is no, the monolith is still the right architecture — and that is not a failure, it is engineering discipline.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Monolith
        M_UI[UI Layer]
        M_Biz[Business Logic]
        M_Data[Data Access]
        M_Jobs[Background Jobs]
        M_DB[(Shared DB)]
        M_UI --> M_Biz --> M_Data --> M_DB
        M_Jobs --> M_Biz
    end
    subgraph Microservices
        C[Client] --> GW[API Gateway]
        GW --> S1[Auth Service]
        GW --> S2[Billing Service]
        GW --> S3[Inventory Service]
        GW --> S4[Recommendation Service]
        S2 --> DB2[(Billing DB)]
        S3 --> DB3[(Inventory DB)]
        S4 --> DB4[(Recs DB)]
        S2 -.sync.-> S3
    end
    style M_DB fill:#fdd
    style GW fill:#ffd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
MONOLITH (one artifact, one process)        MICROSERVICES (N artifacts, N processes)

+-----------------------------------+        +--------+   +----------+
| App Process                       |        | Client |-->| API      |
|  +------+  +------+  +------+     |        +--------+   | Gateway  |
|  | UI   |->| Biz  |->| Data |     |                     +----+-----+
|  +------+  +------+  +------+     |                          |
|     |         |         |         |       +------+----+----+------+
|     +---------+---------+         |       v      v    v    v
|               v                   |     +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+
|         +-----------+             |     |Auth| |Bill| |Inv | |Rec |
|         | Shared DB |             |     +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+
|         +-----------+             |        |      |      |      |
+-----------------------------------+      +v-+   +-v-+   +-v-+  +-v-+
   deploy = 1 artifact                      DB    DB     DB     DB
   failure = all or nothing               deploy = N artifacts
   call latency = nanoseconds             failure = partial (need breakers)
```

### Walkthrough
1. In the monolith, every module shares one process and one database, so a call from UI to Billing to Inventory is a sequence of in-process function calls — fast, but every change ships in one big deploy.
2. In the microservices topology, the client calls the API Gateway, which routes to Auth, Billing, Inventory, and Recommendation services. Each owns its own database and deploys independently.
3. Cross-service calls (e.g., Billing needs Inventory data) go over the network, adding latency and partial-failure risk that must be handled with circuit breakers, retries, and sagas instead of in-process transactions.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Monolith-vs-microservices comparison: service registry mock + deployment metrics.
# Simulates both styles and prints deploy-time, call-latency, and failure-blast metrics.

import random, time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class ServiceMetrics:
    name: str
    deploy_seconds: int          # time to ship a change
    call_latency_ms: float       # cross-call latency
    failure_blast_radius: float  # 0..1 share of system affected by one bug

# --- Monolith: one artifact, in-process calls ---
MONOLITH = ServiceMetrics(
    name="monolith",
    deploy_seconds=1800,         # 30 min coordinated deploy across 8 teams
    call_latency_ms=0.001,       # in-process function call ~1us
    failure_blast_radius=1.0,    # one bug can crash the whole process
)

# --- Microservices: N artifacts, network calls ---
MICRO = [
    ServiceMetrics("auth",  deploy_seconds=120, call_latency_ms=8,   failure_blast_radius=0.10),
    ServiceMetrics("billing", deploy_seconds=300, call_latency_ms=12, failure_blast_radius=0.20),
    ServiceMetrics("inventory", deploy_seconds=180, call_latency_ms=10, failure_blast_radius=0.15),
    ServiceMetrics("recs",  deploy_seconds=90,  call_latency_ms=15,  failure_blast_radius=0.05),
]

def monolith_user_request():
    """In-process call chain: UI -> Biz -> Data. Nanoseconds."""
    return MONOLITH.call_latency_ms * 3   # 3 function calls

def micro_user_request(gateway_overhead_ms=4):
    """Gateway + 4 fan-out calls, summed (best case, parallel)."""
    fan_out = max(s.call_latency_ms for s in MICRO)   # parallel -> max
    return gateway_overhead_ms + fan_out

def simulate_failure(style: str):
    """Roll a random bug; report share of system affected."""
    if style == "monolith":
        return MONOLITH.failure_blast_radius
    return random.choice(MICRO).failure_blast_radius

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"Monolith p50 call latency: {monolith_user_request():.3f} ms")
    print(f"Microservice p50 call latency: {micro_user_request():.1f} ms")
    print(f"Monolith deploy: {MONOLITH.deploy_seconds}s | "
          f"Slowest microservice deploy: {max(s.deploy_seconds for s in MICRO)}s")
    print(f"Monolith failure blast: {simulate_failure('monolith')*100:.0f}% | "
          f"Microservice failure blast: {simulate_failure('micro')*100:.0f}%")
```
